key_claims: Bin Ladin rose as a financier of Arab fighters in the Afghan jihad and in Sudan funded extremists in Bosnia, Egypt, Kashmir, Jordan, Tunisia, Algeria and Yemen.
CIA saw Bin Ladin mainly as a terrorist financier in the early 1990s and only singled him out as a major target in early 1996.
Al-Qa'ida's plotting in the late 1990s depended on the Taliban sanctuary in Afghanistan.
Bin Ladin and the Taliban had a 'terrorist sponsoring a state' relationship, with al-Qa'ida money and fighters supporting the Taliban.
Al-Qa'ida-Taliban camps trained militants who were sent to Kashmir, Chechnya and Bosnia and then dispersed worldwide.
CIA had no regular presence in or access to Afghanistan, which handicapped its efforts.
CIA assessed since 1998-99 that Bin Ladin commanded a global terrorist network targeting US interests worldwide.
In summer 2001 CIA collection indicated intensive al-Qa'ida operational planning, including against the US homeland, but lacked specific date, time or location.
CIA's 1999 operational plan, The Plan, prioritized penetrating al-Qa'ida and capturing Bin Ladin and his lieutenants.
In late 2000 CIA flew unarmed Predator missions over Afghanistan that may have imaged Bin Ladin at Tarnak Farms.
The Taliban detected and launched interceptors against the Predator flights.
